outcome: No accepted or expert-digested change to the problem was found since 26 January 2024. Two unreviewed preprints.org manuscripts (Nov 2025, Jan 2026) claim a full or near-full resolution, but neither has any expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification; the January 2026 claim was withdrawn by its own author for a 'fundamental mathematical issue' before it could be assessed further, and the November 2025 claim's own abstract concedes its main density result is conditional on GRH and that even its unconditional part covers only a narrow case (14-prime, odd-parity composites) that was already excluded by classical bounds (any solution needs ω(n) ≥ 14, so 'eliminating 14-prime composites' does not on its face touch the open cases with more prime factors). A third, October 2025 preprint on a generalized totient-divisibility equation φ(n) = n − a explicitly states that the a = −1 case, i.e. Lehmer's original problem, 'remains one of the oldest open problems' — it is a related/generalizing paper, not a resolution. Wikipedia's live article (checked here only to see if consensus had shifted; not used as a source of fact) still lists the problem as open, citing bounds work through 2019 (Burek and Żmija) with nothing newer.
summary: This problem was triaged as 'likely' on the strength of two preprints.org manuscripts, and I read as much of both as I could reach (the site returns HTTP 403 to automated fetchers, so I worked from cached search snippets, titles, and the searchable text Google/Bing have indexed of each abstract — this is a real gap, noted in `incomplete`). The November 2025 manuscript ('Lehmer's Totient Conjecture: 2-Adic Closure, Computational Certificates, and GRH-Density Resolution') claims to close the conjecture in two stages: an unconditional elimination of '14-prime composites' via 2-adic valuation, and a GRH-conditional density argument for larger configurations. Two problems keep this from counting as a change to the problem as stated. First, scope: since Cohen and Hagis (1980) already proved any solution needs at least 14 distinct prime factors, and later work pushed this bound to roughly 40,000,000 for solutions divisible by 3 (Burcsi–Czirbusz–Farkas), a paper that only 'eliminates 14-prime composites' is working well inside territory already known to be empty or near-empty — it is not clear this narrows the actual open frontier at all, let alone resolves it. Second, even taking the density claim at face value, it is GRH-conditional and, per the triage note and my own searching, has not been read or endorsed by any expert; there is no journal acceptance, no digestion on Tao's blog, MathOverflow, or any number-theory survey, and no arXiv posting at all — it exists only as an unreviewed preprints.org manuscript. The January 2026 manuscript ('A Short Proof the Lehmer's Totient Problem Has No Solutions') claimed a complete, unconditional resolution but was withdrawn by its own author on or around 15 January 2026 for a 'fundamental mathematical issue,' before any outside verification occurred — a textbook incident rather than a result. A third, related preprint from October 2025 ('The Euler Totient Divisibility Problem: a Complete Classification') studies the generalized equation φ(n) = n − a for general integer a and explicitly identifies a = −1 (Lehmer's own problem) as remaining open; it resolves other values of a but is a related problem under §3.1, not a case of this one. I also checked whether any AI system was involved in producing either claim: no methods section, acknowledgement, or third-party report surfaces any authorial statement of AI-generated mathematics for either preprint, so ai_role is 'none' by default (no basis_quote is possible). I found and briefly checked pith.science, an AI-assisted preprint-review platform, but it has not reviewed either of these two manuscripts, so it provides no independent verification either way. Net: this problem still merits `open` with `no_change_found`, though the January 2026 withdrawal event is itself the sort of instructive incident this format wants preserved, so I have described it in `summary` and left it out of `event` because it never became a serious claim that a status other than `open` could rest on.
competing_reading: One could argue the withdrawn January 2026 preprint deserves its own `progress`/`incident` classification with `event.kind` 'preprint' dated 2026-01, on the model of §7's 'a withdrawn claim is still an event.' I chose `open`/`no_change_found` instead because, unlike the withdrawn-claim examples the instructions have in mind (a claim that got far enough to be read and then retracted), this one appears to have been withdrawn essentially immediately, with no evidence any outside mathematician engaged with it before the withdrawal — there is nothing here beyond 'someone posted and then un-posted a claim,' which is weaker than an announced-then-withdrawn result. If a reviewer disagrees, the correct fix is `status: progress`, `resolution_direction: null`, `ai_role: incident` is NOT appropriate regardless (that code is reserved for AI-produced claims specifically, and no AI involvement was found here) — so at most this would become `progress` with `ai_role: none`.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation (or refutation) by a number theorist of the November 2025 manuscript's 2-adic and bounded-catch arguments — e.g. a MathOverflow thread, a referee report, or a follow-up preprint citing and checking it — would resolve whether any real progress underlies that claim. Access to the full text of both preprints.org manuscripts (currently blocked to automated fetching) would also let a future pass verify the scope question directly rather than relying on abstract-level snippets.
